payout_quote: Recalls.gov: six federal agencies 'have joined together to create Recalls.gov — a "one stop shop" for U.S. Government recalls.' Recalls find SAFETY REMEDIES for products you already own (refund, repair, or replacement per the recall notice) — this is not income and pays nothing if you do not own a recalled product.
timing: Search is instant. Remedies follow each recall notice's instructions — often a return to the store where purchased or direct contact with the manufacturer; you usually do not need a receipt.
biggest_catch: Recalls are product-safety remedies, not money-making — the 'payout' is a refund, repair, or replacement of something you already bought. You must own (or have bought) the specific recalled product, model, and date range; most searches confirm your products are fine.
eligibility: Anyone who owns or purchased a recalled product. Each recall notice states the exact product identifiers (brand, model, batch, date range) and the remedy.
steps: Go to https://www.recalls.gov/ and use Recent Recalls or Search for Recalls (by agency/product type) to check products you own — especially children's products, appliances, and secondhand purchases.
Match your product exactly against the recall notice: brand, model number, batch/lot codes, and date range.
Follow the recall notice's remedy instructions: return to the store, contact the manufacturer, or stop using the product as directed.
Sign up for recall email alerts from the relevant agencies so future recalls reach you.
catches: Not income — remedies are refund/repair/replacement of products you already own.
You must match the exact recalled product identifiers; a similar-looking product may not be covered.
Recall remedies differ per notice — read it carefully (some medical-device recalls mean check/adjust, not return).
Safety recalls do not expire, so check secondhand and hand-me-down items too.
notes: Verified 2026-09-22/23: recalls.gov is live (crawled within the hour), run as the joint portal of CPSC, FDA, NHTSA, EPA, US Coast Guard, and USDA. In-app, this route belongs in the recovery lane and must be framed as product-safety remedies, never as income. No app — website only.
